```{python}
from research_site import Study

study = Study()
LANGUAGES = ["Language X", "Language Y", "Language Z"]
STAGES = ["No related language"] + [f"{n} related language{'s' if n > 1 else ''}" for n in range(1, 7)]
```

## Summary

- We tested whether fine-tuning a model on related languages first, then on the target language, improves translation of low-resource languages.
- **It did not help for any of the three languages tested.** In every case, BLEU after the final fine-tuning on the target language was below the baseline with no related language.
- BLEU tended to fall further as more related languages were added: by 2.4 points for Language X with six related languages, 1.9 for Language Y with three, and 3.0 for Language Z with five.
- These are single runs without intervals, so small differences may be noise.

## The question

Low-resource languages have little training text. Related languages may share vocabulary and grammar with the target, so training on them first could give the model a better starting point. We asked whether this staged approach improves the target language's translations, and whether adding more related languages helps more.

## How it was tested

<!-- REVIEW: the base model, the test set and its size, and the staging details are not stated in the source spreadsheet. Please add them (which model; which languages and how much text per stage; how many verses are in each test set). -->

A model is fine-tuned on one related language, then on a second, and so on, one stage per related language. After the last stage it is fine-tuned on the target language (the final fine-tune), using default training settings with no early stopping. The baseline skips the related-language stages. We repeated this for one to six related languages for Languages X and Z, and one to three for Language Y, and scored the model after the final fine-tune with BLEU on the target language's test set.

## Results

```{python}
#| renderings: [light, dark]
study.bar_chart("BLEU", groups=STAGES, systems=LANGUAGES, x_title="BLEU after final fine-tune (higher is better)", x_range=(0, 25))
```

```{python}
study.table(measures=["BLEU"], groups=LANGUAGES, systems=STAGES, digits=2, intervals=False, measure_column=False, group_title="Language")
```

Every staged run scores below its language's baseline. The gap grows as related languages are added, though not at every step: for Language Z, six related languages (13.44) score slightly above five (13.10). Language X scores identically (18.68) with two and three related languages, and we have not determined why.

## Limitations

- **Single runs, no intervals.** Differences of one to three BLEU points could be within the noise between runs.
- **Three languages, one metric.** Only BLEU was recorded, and Language Y was tested with up to three related languages.
- **Unexplained result.** The identical Language X scores for two and three related languages have not been investigated.
- **Scope.** A parallel set of experiments that used LoRA is not part of this study.
